blocks.content: Manipur possesses one of North-East India's longest continuously documented royal chronicles - the Cheitharol Kumbaba - giving its ancient and medieval history an unusually well-recorded character compared to many neighbouring hill states.
The Cheitharol Kumbaba & the Ningthouja Dynasty

Manipur's traditional royal chronicle, the Cheitharol Kumbaba ('Royal Chronicle of Manipur'), records a continuous line of Meitei kings beginning traditionally from 33 CE with King Nongda Lairen Pakhangba, founder of the Ningthouja dynasty - making this one of the longest continuously documented royal chronicles anywhere in India, maintained and updated across many centuries.

The historical kingdom, known to the Meitei as 'Kangleipak' (and to outsiders historically as 'Manipur', a name popularised particularly from the medieval period onward, possibly linked to Hindu Vaishnavite influence associating the land with mythological/puranic associations), was centred on the Imphal Valley, with successive rulers gradually extending influence into the surrounding hill areas over the centuries.

The Meitei kingdom's early religious tradition centred on Sanamahism, an indigenous animist-monotheistic faith with its own cosmology and ritual practices, which remained the dominant faith of the Meitei people until a major religious transformation in the 18th century (below).

★ EXAM POINT: The Cheitharol Kumbaba traditionally traces the Ningthouja dynasty back to 33 CE with King Pakhangba - a frequently tested 'earliest ruler/founding date' fact for Manipur, comparable in exam significance to founding-dynasty facts tested for other Indian regional kingdoms.

A pivotal religious and cultural transformation occurred in the early 18th century under King Pamheiba (also known by his Hindu title Garibniwaz, reigned 1709-1748), who adopted Vaishnavite Hinduism as the state religion, promoted by Bengali Vaishnavite gurus, leading to widespread conversion of the Meitei population from Sanamahism to Hinduism over subsequent decades.

This conversion had lasting cultural consequences still visible today: it introduced Bengali-script-derived writing conventions for a period (though the indigenous Meitei Mayek script has since been revived, Chapter 8), reshaped Meitei social/caste practices along Hindu lines, and laid the cultural foundation for Manipur's globally renowned Vaishnavite performance tradition, Manipuri classical dance (Chapter 9).

Despite this widespread conversion, a Sanamahi revival movement has gained increasing prominence among Meitei communities in more recent decades, seeking to preserve and reassert the indigenous pre-Hindu faith and cultural identity alongside or in place of Vaishnavite Hindu practice.

★ EXAM POINT: King Garibniwaz's early-18th-century conversion to Vaishnavite Hinduism is the single most important religious-transformation event in Meitei history - remember it directly explains both Manipur's historically strong Vaishnavite-Hindu identity AND the origins of the globally celebrated Manipuri classical dance tradition (Chapter 9).

Manipur's kingdom faced repeated and highly destructive invasions by the Konbaung dynasty of neighbouring Burma (Myanmar) through the 18th and early 19th centuries, culminating in a prolonged Burmese occupation of Manipur from 1819 to 1826 - a traumatic period remembered in Manipuri historical memory as the 'Seven Years' Devastation' (Chahi Taret Khuntakpa), during which large parts of the population fled or were displaced and the kingdom's administration was severely disrupted.

This Burmese occupation ended only with British intervention: the Treaty of Yandabo (1826), which concluded the First Anglo-Burmese War, restored Manipuri sovereignty (under British protection/suzerainty) and returned Gambhir Singh to the Manipuri throne - marking the beginning of a British-protected-state relationship that would shape Manipur's subsequent 19th-century political trajectory.

★ EXAM POINT: The 'Seven Years' Devastation' (Chahi Taret Khuntakpa, 1819-1826) refers specifically to the Burmese occupation of Manipur - ended by the Treaty of Yandabo (1826), the same treaty that concluded the First Anglo-Burmese War more broadly. This treaty is a useful cross-topic link to wider British-Burma colonial history.

items: Cheitharol Kumbaba = Manipur's traditional royal chronicle; records the Ningthouja dynasty from 33 CE (King Pakhangba) - one of India's longest continuous royal chronicles.
Meitei kingdom traditionally known as 'Kangleipak'; original faith was Sanamahism (indigenous animist-monotheistic tradition).
King Pamheiba/Garibniwaz (r. 1709-1748) converted the Meitei to Vaishnavite Hinduism, laying the cultural basis for Manipuri classical dance.
'Seven Years' Devastation' (Chahi Taret Khuntakpa, 1819-1826) = Burmese occupation of Manipur, ended by the Treaty of Yandabo (1826), which also concluded the First Anglo-Burmese War.
